English Wikipedia says only that the Romans founded the settlement and that its nature is uncertain; roman-britain.co.uk, the Tadcaster Town Council page and German Wikipedia (Tadcaster) give no founding year or century for Calcaria, and the one 4th-century date in the article belongs to the fort at Newton Kyme, not to Calcaria. The one source that turns the bins into a 'circa 1000 BC' start is Grokipedia, an AI-written site that is excluded, and it admits no datable material. No reputable source dates the start of this site.

The Roman Emperors Route (Itinerarium Romanum Serbiae) is, per English Wikipedia, 'a tourism and archaeology project in Serbia, a route spanning 600 km with several ancient Roman sites'. It is a modern itinerary linking separate sites (Sirmium, Singidunum, Viminacium, Felix Romuliana, Naissus and others), so it has no single centre or main monument; its Wikidata item has no coordinate and no page gives a point for it. The stored point (Belgrade) is not a point of the route as such. No source can be quoted for the site's point.

The Roman Emperors Route is a present-day tourism and archaeology project, not an ancient site with a construction or first occupation; the Roman sites it links begin at very different dates, and no source dates a start of the route itself. The stored -500 is a band edge made by a rule, with no source behind it.

Wikipedia says only that the complex was influenced by the Wari and Chanka cultures, with no date. MINCETUR's inventory record for the Complejo Arqueologico de Caniche (ficha 1267) calls it a Pre-Inca complex of 'el Horizonte Intermedio' (a phrase that is not one of the standard periods: it matches neither the Early nor the Late Intermediate Period) and lists Huarpa, Rukana, Chanka and Wari occupation followed by the Inca. That names several successive cultures, none as the site's first, and no year, century or single vocabulary period for the start, so no start can be quoted; the stored 500 is a band-edge value.

The sources disagree on when Cardiccia (Sartene) starts. Wikipedia's Prehistory of Corsica lists it among Middle Neolithic sites (5000-4000 BC) without a per-site reference, the Museo dei Dolmen archaeoastronomy table gives 2800 B.C. for the dolmen's stellar alignment (Proverbio and Calledda 2004), and the one scholarly mention found (Ateliers du LESC 2000) gives only a 'supposed' 4th-millennium date for the lithic finds and doubts the tomb is that old. The Cardiccia Wikipedia stub, Wikidata and the tourism pages give no date. Sources in conflict across two buckets leave no single start that can be stated, so unresolved.
